title: Are Implants Right for Me?
meta_title: Am I a Candidate for Dental Implants? | West Alexandria Dental Care
meta_description: Implant candidacy explained: bone volume, gum health, smoking, diabetes, medications, age and general health; what the consultation and 3D scan evaluate.
h1: Are dental implants right for you?
intro: Most adults missing a tooth can have an implant. The exceptions matter, though, and they are better found at a consultation than after a failed implant. Here is what we weigh, what the 3D scan shows, and what the alternatives are when the honest answer is not yet, or not this way.

sections.heading: What makes a good candidate
items: Enough bone, in height and width, where the implant would go, or bone that can be rebuilt with a graft.
Healthy gums, or gum disease that has been treated and is stable.
General health that allows minor surgery and normal healing.
No smoking, or a willingness to stop around the time of surgery and healing.
Jaw growth complete, which for most people means late teens or older.
A commitment to daily cleaning and regular check-ups afterward.

sections.heading: The factors we look at closely

items.title: Bone
items.body: Bone shrinks after a tooth is lost. The cone-beam CT scan measures exactly what is there. Too little usually means a graft first, not a refusal.

items.title: Gum disease
items.body: The bacteria that loosen teeth will loosen an implant. Active periodontitis is treated and stabilized before any implant is placed.

items.title: Smoking
items.body: Smoking roughly doubles the failure rate during healing and raises the risk of gum problems around implants later. We say so plainly and talk about timing.

items.title: Diabetes
items.body: Well-controlled diabetes is compatible with implants. Poorly controlled diabetes slows healing and raises infection risk, so control comes first, with your physician.

items.title: Medications
items.body: Bone-strengthening drugs such as bisphosphonates, some cancer treatments, long-term steroids and anticoagulants all change the plan. Bring your full list.

items.title: Other conditions
items.body: Previous radiation to the jaw, uncontrolled autoimmune disease, heavy grinding and certain heart conditions need discussion and sometimes a conversation with your doctor.

items.title: History
items.body: Your health, medications, habits and what you want the result to do for you.

items.title: Examination
items.body: The gap, the neighboring teeth, your bite, your gums, and how much room there is for a crown.

items.title: 3D scan
items.body: A cone-beam CT shows bone volume and density, and the position of the nerve in the lower jaw and the sinus in the upper. This is the step that turns a guess into a plan.

items.title: A written plan
items.body: Whether an implant is advisable, whether grafting is needed, how many visits, the timeline and the cost, with the alternatives beside it. No pressure to decide on the day.

sections.heading: When there is not enough bone
body: Bone can often be rebuilt. A small graft at the time of extraction preserves the socket. A graft placed a few months before the implant can widen a thin ridge. In the upper back jaw, where the sinus sits close, a sinus lift adds bone beneath it. Each adds time and cost, and each is explained before you commit. For some people the amount of grafting needed tips the balance toward a bridge or a partial denture instead, and we say so.

sections.heading: If implants are not the answer
sections.body: A bridge, a partial denture or a full denture may serve you better, or serve you now while implants are planned for later. None of these is a consolation prize; each is the right tool for particular mouths. The decision guide sets them side by side.

faqs.q: Is there an upper age limit?
faqs.a: No. Implants are placed successfully in people in their eighties and nineties. Bone, health and medications matter; birthdays do not.
Not until jaw growth is complete, usually late teens for girls and a little later for boys, because an implant does not move with a growing jaw. A temporary replacement bridges the gap until then.

faqs.q: I have had gum disease. Can I still have implants?
faqs.a: Yes, once it is treated and stable, with a commitment to periodontal maintenance afterward. Untreated gum disease is the single biggest reason implants fail later.

faqs.q: I take a blood thinner. Is that a problem?
faqs.a: Usually not. Most implant placements are done without stopping anticoagulants, using local measures to control bleeding, and we coordinate with your physician. Never stop a blood thinner on your own.

faqs.q: What if my tooth has been missing for years?
faqs.a: An implant is still often possible. The scan shows how much bone remains. If it has shrunk, a graft can usually rebuild it, and the plan accounts for the extra step.

cta.heading: Find out with a scan, not a guess.
cta.body: Book an implant consultation. The 3D scan and exam answer the question in one visit, and you leave with a written plan either way.
